W4405407480.a1.text: The modal collapse argument claims divine simplicity forces God to necessarily create whatever He creates and creatures to necessarily perform their actions.
W4405407480.a1.quote: The modal collapse argument states that the traditional doctrine of divine simplicity entails that God necessarily creates whatever he creates and also that all creatures necessarily perform whatever actions they perform.

W4405407480.a2.text: Responding to modal collapse requires that part of the truthmaker linking God to contingent facts be extrinsic, locating contingency there.
W4405407480.a2.quote: Section 1 explains why responding to the modal collapse argument requires that part of the truthmaker relating God to contingent facts be extrinsic to God, and that it is only in this part that contingency lies.

W4405407480.a3.text: The paper defends a general view of action where such properties can be at least partially extrinsic.
W4405407480.a3.quote: This paper argues for a general view of action, in which such properties can turn out to be at least partially extrinsic.

W4405407480.c001.text: If God is simple, then God has no intrinsic accidental or contingent properties.
W4405407480.c001.quote: (i) If God is simple, God has no intrinsic accidental or contingent properties;

W4405407480.c002.text: It is an intrinsic property of God to have freely chosen to create the actual world and to know everything about the contingent individual creatures He creates.
W4405407480.c002.quote: (ii) it is an intrinsic property of God (a) to have freely chosen to create the actual world and (b) to know everything about the contingent individual creatures he creates;

W4405407480.c003.text: If God freely chooses to create the actual world, then it is contingent that God created it and that He created it exactly as He did.
W4405407480.c003.quote: (iii) if God freely chooses to create the actual world, it is contingent that God created it and that he created it exactly the way he created it;

W4405407480.c004.text: If individual creatures are contingently created by God, then any knowledge about them is knowledge of contingent facts and therefore a contingent knowledge.
W4405407480.c004.quote: (iv) if individual creatures are contingently created by God, any knowledge about them is a knowledge of contingent facts and therefore a contingent knowledge;

W4405407480.c005.text: Therefore the properties of freely choosing to create the world and knowing everything about contingent creatures are intrinsic properties that God contingently has.
W4405407480.c005.quote: (v) (a) and (b) are intrinsic properties that God contingently has;

W4405407480.c006.text: Therefore God has intrinsic accidental properties.

W4405407480.c008.text: The modal collapse argument is probably the most difficult objection to the doctrine of divine simplicity.
W4405407480.c008.quote: Among objections to the doctrine of divine simplicity (DDS) frequently discussed in recent literature, the so called “modal collapse argument” is probably the more difficult one.

W4405407480.c009.text: A satisfactory solution to the modal collapse argument requires a theory of volition and knowledge where properties (a) and (b) are extrinsic, thus denying premise (1)(ii).
W4405407480.c009.quote: A satisfactory solution to (1) requires a theory of volition and knowledge where properties (a) and (b), are extrinsic properties, i.e. denying premise (1)(ii).

W4405407480.c010.text: The asymmetry thesis states that the relationship from creature to creator is real, while the relationship from creator to creature is only of reason.
W4405407480.c010.quote: (2) Asymmetry thesis. The relationship that goes from the creature to the creator is real, but the correlative relationship that goes from the creator to the creature is only of reason.

W4405407480.c011.text: If a is really related by R to b but there is no foundation in b of the same type as a’s foundation for R to b, then there is no real correlation R′ in b, and R and R′ are non‑mutual.
W4405407480.c011.quote: If a is really related by R to b, but there is no foundation in b of the same type as a’s foundation for R to b, then there is no real corelation R’ in b, and R and R’ are non-mutual

W4405407480.c012.text: Divine simplicity requires that all non‑tautological truths only about God have only God himself as their minimal truthmaker.
W4405407480.c012.quote: divine simplicity requires that all non-tautological truths that are only about God, have only God himself as their minimal truthmaker (Pruss 2008, 152–54).

W4405407480.c013.text: Any correct attribution to God of an accidental property has as its truthmaker God and something contingent besides God, so the property is at least partially extrinsic.
W4405407480.c013.quote: any correct attribution to God of an accidental property has as its truthmaker God and something contingent besides God, and hence the property is at least in part extrinsic

W4405407480.c014.text: The truth of the proposition ‘God freely chooses to create the actual world’ depends on the conjunction of a necessary fact about God and a contingent fact about the world.
W4405407480.c014.quote: (4) Partial extrinsicness of divine volition of the contingent. What makes true the proposition “God freely chooses to create the actual world” is the conjunction of a necessary fact about God and a contingent fact about the world.

W4405407480.c015.text: God’s relation to the world is partially based on facts extrinsic to God, not on contingent intrinsic facts.
W4405407480.c015.quote: Partial extrinsicness of God's relation to the world. The relations between God and the world are at least partially based on facts that are extrinsic to God, and are not based on contingent facts intrinsic to God.

W4405407480.c016.text: God freely chooses to create the actual world because a necessary fact about God combines with a contingent fact about the world.
W4405407480.c016.quote: Partial extrinsicness of divine volition of the contingent. What makes true the proposition “God freely chooses to create the actual world” is the conjunction of a necessary fact about God and a contingent fact about the world.

W4405407480.c017.text: God knows the actions of free agents because a necessary fact about God combines with a contingent fact about created free agents.
W4405407480.c017.quote: Partial extrinsicness of divine knowledge of contingent particulars. What makes true the proposition “God knows the actions performed by free agents” is the conjunction of a necessary fact about God and a contingent fact about created free agents.

W4405407480.c018.text: Accepting hypotheses (4) and (5) denies that God possesses any accidental intrinsic properties.
W4405407480.c018.quote: Accepting hypotheses (4) and (5) entails denying (1) (ii), because (a) and (b) can turn out true without involving any accidental intrinsic properties of God whatsoever.

W4405407480.c019.text: The general hypothesis (3) lets us dismiss any other variant of the modal collapse argument.
W4405407480.c019.quote: Further on, the more general hypothesis (3) allows us to dismiss any other possible variant of the argument of modal collapse.

W4405407480.c020.text: Aquinas’ claim that cognitive and volitional acts are immanent makes (4) and (5) implausible because their truthmakers would have to be intrinsic to God.
W4405407480.c020.quote: However, there are some obvious reasons to consider (4) and (5) implausible. Aquinas himself is emphatic about the immanent character that cognitive and volitional acts have.

W4405407480.c021.text: We only need to show that volitional and cognitive acts are partially extrinsic, with contingency arising from external facts rather than God’s immanent act.
W4405407480.c021.quote: Let us remember, however, that we do not need to demonstrate that such volitional and cognitive acts are entirely extrinsic. Instead, we need only to show that they are partially so, and that the contingency involved arises solely from a contingent fact about the external object willed or known (not from the agent’s or knower’s immanent act).

W4405407480.c022.text: Causal relations always require a property in the effect, and a property in the cause only when the cause gains perfection from the effect.
W4405407480.c022.quote: Causal relations requiring real properties in both relata. Causal relations always require positing something within the effect (the acted, moved, or effected) but only require positing something in the cause (the mover, or the agent) when the latter obtains some perfection from the occurrence of the effect.

W4405407480.c023.text: Parsimony demands that we do not posit more real properties than are strictly necessary to ground a relation.
W4405407480.c023.quote: This idea can be defended on simple grounds of explanatory economics. Parsimony requires us not to posit any more real properties than those strictly necessary to properly ground the relation.

W4405407480.c024.text: Grant argues that assuming an intrinsic property of a cause either makes the effect non‑contingent or adds another contingent fact, undermining cosmological arguments.
W4405407480.c024.quote: Grant shows that if we assume that in order to make sense of a’s causally accounting for b there must be some real or intrinsic property or feature of a that would not be there were a not causing b, then this intrinsic feature or property of a must either be necessary or contingent.

W4405407480.c025.text: Defending DDS against (1) requires the same assumption needed to defend libertarian free will.
W4405407480.c025.quote: This last claim is important, because we must remember that vindicating libertarian free agency is one of the main motivations frequently invoked for the rejection of DDS.

W4405407480.c026.text: To overcome difficulty (1) we must extend the gratuitousness of God’s creative act to its ultimate consequences.
W4405407480.c026.quote: Therefore, in order to overcome difficulty (1), instead of denying the absolutely gratuitous character of God’s creative act, what we have to do is to carry this gratuitousness to its ultimate consequences.

W4405407480.c027.text: The precise content of a volitional act need not be an intrinsic feature of the agent.
W4405407480.c027.quote: There are good reasons to think that the precise content of a volitional act need not be an intrinsic feature of the agent.

W4405407480.c028.text: For any agent, the truthmaker of a free choice is the conjunction of an intrinsic desire and an extrinsic fact about the produced effect.
W4405407480.c028.quote: Partial extrinsicness of any volition. For any agent a who freely produces an effect x, the truthmaker of the proposition “a freely chooses to produce x” is the conjunction between (i) an intrinsic fact about a, consisting in the internal desire of end q, that can be equally fulfilled by performing a range of various actions, one of which involves producing x; (ii) a fact about x, consisting in the production of x being the precise action freely performed by a.

W4405407480.c029.text: (7)(ii) is a fact extrinsic to the agent and can be contingent without undermining God's absolute simplicity.
W4405407480.c029.quote: (7)(ii) is a fact extrinsic to the agent and can therefore be contingent without undermining God’s absolute simplicity.

W4405407480.c030.text: God's volition to create the world is not a causal relationship where the cause attains perfection from the effect, as described in scenario (6).
W4405407480.c030.quote: The key point to keep in mind is that this is not one of the scenarios described in (6)—a type of causal relationship where the cause attains a certain perfection from the occurrence of the effect.

W4405407480.c031.text: Aquinas holds that in a single act of volition God wills his own essence and also wills creatures, ordering the latter to the former as manifestations of his goodness, not because they contribute to his perfection.
W4405407480.c031.quote: Thomas Aquinas considered that in a single act of volition God wills his own essence and also wills the creatures. He wills the latter ordered to the former, and not insofar as they contribute in some way to his own perfection, but rather as manifestations of his goodness.

W4405407480.c032.text: Miller argues that situation (c) most resembles God's volitional act, where objects are willed as ordered to one another as manifestations rather than as independent means or ends.
W4405407480.c032.quote: Miller argues that situation (c) is the one that most resembles God’s volitional act.

W4405407480.c033.text: In situation (c), the object of Mary's volitional act can vary without altering Mary's intrinsic state.
W4405407480.c033.quote: For this reason, the object of Mary’s volitional act can vary without altering Mary’s intrinsic stat.

W4405407480.c034.text: If God's purpose in loving creatures is sharing his goodness, any world could fulfill it, so the particular world created does not require a new volitional act; its contingency makes it the object of the necessary divine volition.
W4405407480.c034.quote: If God’s purpose in loving creatures is sharing his own goodness, this purpose could be perfectly fulfilled by creating a world completely different from ours, or even without any world being created at all.

W4405407480.c035.text: The description is compatible with Aquinas's claim that divine willing of contingent creatures includes their contingency.
W4405407480.c035.quote: This description is compatible with Aquinas’s claim that divine willing of contingent creatures includes their contingency (e. g., Summa Theologiae I q.19 a.8).

W4405407480.c036.text: Aquinas does not argue that the particular contingent creatures created by God are included in God's internal volition; only the general contingent nature is.
W4405407480.c036.quote: When claiming so, Aquinas does not argue that the particular contingent creatures created by God are included in God’s internal volition.

W4405407480.c037.text: The contingency of the effect is due to indeterminacy in the prior volition and does not require any concurrent secondary causes.
W4405407480.c037.quote: In my argument, the contingency of the effect is due to indeterminacy in the prior volition and does not require any concurrent secondary causes.

W4405407480.c038.text: One might argue that God's love must reach each creature's unique individuality, implying something within God beyond the single necessary love of his essence.
W4405407480.c038.quote: Someone might argue that God’s love for creatures is meant to reach them in their unique individuality, and therefore involves positing within God something more than the single necessary love of his own essence which manifests itself by extending indistinctly to the entire universe of possible creatures through which God could have freely shared his goodness.

W4405407480.c039.text: Palamas' distinction between divine essence and energeiai can be compatible with divine simplicity if energeiai merely modify God's love by referring to concrete objects without positing intrinsic contingent properties.
W4405407480.c039.quote: All of this can be compatible with DDS as long as we insist that the energeiai do not posit an intrinsic contingent property on God himself, but simply modify his love intentionally by referring it to a concrete object as terminus of the loving relation.

W4405407480.c040.text: Should the difficulty of content externalism for divine knowledge lead us to conclude that God cannot know contingent individuals?
W4405407480.c040.quote: Should such considerations lead us to conclude that God cannot know contingent individuals?

W4405407480.c041.text: Partial extrinsicness of divine speculative knowledge holds that 'God knows x' is true when (i) an intrinsic necessary fact about God exists and (ii) x exists as a particular creature.
W4405407480.c041.quote: (8) Partial extrinsicness of divine speculative knowledge. Whenever God knows a particular creature x, what makes true the proposition “God knows x” is the conjunction between (i) an intrinsic necessary fact about God, consisting in the divine essence being such as to speculatively know whatever happens to be the case without suffering any intrinsic change depending on the precise content of his knowledge; and (ii) a fact about x, consisting in x being the case, and therefore x being among those things that God knows.

W4405407480.c042.text: Partial extrinsicness of any fabricative knowledge holds that 'a knows x' is true when (i) the agent has intrinsic self‑knowledge including the chosen effect and (ii) x is the precise effect the agent freely produced.
W4405407480.c042.quote: (9) Partial extrinsicness of any fabricative knowledge. For any agent a who freely produces an effect x, what makes true the proposition “a knows x” is the conjunction between (i) an intrinsic fact about the agent, consisting in the agent’s self‑knowledge, which includes whatever the agent freely chooses to produce; and (ii) a fact about x, consisting in x being the precise effect the agent has chosen to produce.

W4405407480.c043.text: Fabricative knowledge is possible because intentionally producing something gives the producer a certain knowledge of that thing.
W4405407480.c043.quote: Fabricative knowledge is possible because the intentional production of something grants a certain knowledge of it.

W4405407480.c044.text: Non‑speculative‑observational knowledge, defended by Anscombe, is a central element of Aristotelian and Thomistic philosophy.
W4405407480.c044.quote: The existence of this knowledge that is not speculative-observational was lucidly defended by Anscombe (1963), and it constitutes a central element in both Aristotelian and Thomistic thought.

W4405407480.c045.text: Musicians know the notes already played because that knowledge arises from the performance itself, not from observation.
W4405407480.c045.quote: However, it is obvious that musicians know all the notes already played, since otherwise they would not know which note to play next. This knowledge of the part of the piece played so far does not have an observational source but arises from the very performance of the action.

W4405407480.c046.text: Human agents lack full self‑transparency; they have only partial awareness of the concrete choices they make and never fully know the precise effects.
W4405407480.c046.quote: Human agents lack full self‑transparency regarding their own actions: They have partial awareness of the concrete choices they have made, but they never have complete knowledge of the precise effects brought about by their decisions.

W4405407480.c047.text: External commitment to precise effects acts as a constraint that agents must be aware of simply by knowing themselves and their freely performed actions.
W4405407480.c047.quote: Though this commitment is not something intrinsic to agents, it nevertheless acts as a constraint of which agents should be aware by the sole fact of knowing themselves and being aware of the actions they have freely performed.

W4405407480.c048.text: The external commitment described can be associated with the theological concept of a covenant.
W4405407480.c048.quote: It is intriguing to associate such external commitment with what theistic religions have historically described as a “covenant”.

W4405407480.c049.quote: Can such accounts be coherent and convincing?

W4405407480.c050.quote: Do they conflict with traditional religious doctrines, such as free will or moral responsibility?

W4405407480.c051.quote: The idea of a God whose knowledge and creation of the precise creatures he makes is not an intrinsic feature might seem, at first glance, monstrously cold and alien to classical theism.

W4405407480.c052.text: A broader examination of underlying theories of action and knowledge is worthwhile for discussions of divine simplicity and modal collapse.
W4405407480.c052.quote: a broader examination of underlying theories of action and knowledge might also be worthwhile.

W4405407480.arg1.mp.text: If God's relation to the world is partially based on facts extrinsic to God, then the accidental properties at issue, volition and knowledge, must be extrinsic.

W4405407480.arg1.r1.text: The truthmaker for 'God freely chooses to create the actual world' is God alone, with the contingent world-fact entering only as the content of the choice rather than as a distinct truthmaking component, and c013 and c015 are restated in terms of extrinsic content rather than extrinsic truthmakers.

W4405407480.arg1.r2.text: If the truthmaker of God's accidental volitional property includes a contingent fact about the world, then that property is extrinsic to God, whatever its origin in God's nature.

W4405407480.arg1.r3.text: If the truthmaker of God's accidental volitional property includes a contingent world-fact only as the content of the volition, then that property is extrinsic to God in the sense that its content depends on something contingent, while its realizer remains wholly divine.

objections.text: Take a case: God wills from eternity that the sun shine on Tuesday. Attribute to God the accidental property 'is such that the sun shines on Tuesday.' Claimed truthmaker: God plus the sun's contingent shining. But consider a divine act of willing identical with God, whose content is fixed by God alone. Suppose the contingent sun-fact merely satisfies that content when the object obtains; it does not contribute to what God is or to what the attribution ascribes. The truth 'God wills that the sun shine on Tuesday' then has God as its sole truthmaker, while 'the sun shines on Tuesday' is a separate truth about the sun. The attribution requires a contingent condition for satisfaction, not a contingent truthmaker-part. So the step from 'a contingent item is needed for truth' to 'the property is partly extrinsic' does not hold.
objections.premise_fails_because: Premise c013 fails because it infers that an accidental attribution is partly extrinsic from a contingent item appearing in its truth-conditions, though that item may only satisfy a content fixed wholly by God's necessary volition.

objections.text: c015 performs a scope shift from semantic truthmaking to ontological grounding. c014 states only that the proposition 'God freely chooses to create the actual world' is true in virtue of a necessary fact about God plus a contingent fact about the world. c015 converts this into the claim that God's relation to the world is based on facts extrinsic to God, not on contingent intrinsic facts. But the world's role as a truthmaker for a relational proposition does not show that the relation is ontologically grounded in extrinsic facts; it shows only that the proposition is about a relation. God's own act of will could be the contingent intrinsic fact that grounds the relation, with the world serving merely as the relatum. c015 assumes without argument that any proposition requiring the world for its truth must track an extrinsically based property, conflating relational semantics with extrinsic ontology.
objections.premise_fails_because: Premise c015 fails because it illicitly shifts from the proposition's relational truthmaker to the claim that God's relation is ontologically based on extrinsic facts, ignoring that an intrinsic act of will could ground the relation.

objections.text: Consider the truth "God is not a body." This is non-tautological and concerns only God. Its minimal truthmaker is the absence of corporeal composition in God—a privative fact, not God himself. Privations are not identical to the entities they characterize: the absence of matter in God is not God, just as the absence of cracks in a vase is not the vase. Divine simplicity requires only that God lack internal metaphysical composition; it imposes no requirement on what makes negative truths about God true. A defender of divine simplicity can fully accept that "God is not a body" is made true by a privation while maintaining that God is absolutely simple. The same applies to "God is not temporal" and "God is not evil"—each is a non-tautological truth only about God whose truthmaker is an absence rather than God himself.
objections.premise_fails_because: Premise W4405407480.c012 fails because it conflates divine simplicity—a thesis about God's lack of composition—with the distinct claim that God is the minimal truthmaker for every non-tautological truth about God, including negative truths whose truthmakers are privations rather than God himself.

objections.text: Consider a craftsman shaping clay: the difficulty of an objection to their method is not measured by the complexity of the tool but by the resistance of the material. Here, the 'difficulty' of the modal collapse argument is likened to the tool, but the premise assumes that the most challenging objection must arise from the internal structure of the doctrine itself. Yet, in practice, the hardest objections often come from external constraints, like the compatibility of divine simplicity with observed contingency. The premise mistakes the source of difficulty, assuming it must be intrinsic rather than arising from external pressures.
objections.premise_fails_because: W4405407480.c008 fails because it incorrectly assumes the most difficult objection must stem from the doctrine's internal structure rather than external constraints.

objections.text: The premise assumes that the truth of 'God freely chooses to create the actual world' requires a contingent fact about the world as a distinct truthmaking component alongside a necessary fact about God. But the smuggled assumption is that this proposition is not wholly a truth about God. It is: it asserts something about God's act of choosing. The premise needs the contingent world-fact to make the truthmaker extrinsic (feeding c013 and c015), yet c012 states that all non-tautological truths only about God have only God as their minimal truthmaker. The proposition 'God freely chooses to create the actual world' is a truth only about God—it predicates a choice of God. To split its truthmaker into a God-component and a world-component is to treat it as a truth partly about the world, which contradicts its grammatical and metaphysical subject. The argument cannot have the contingent world-fact as a truthmaker for this proposition without violating c012, yet it needs that contingent fact to generate the extrinsic relation in c013 and c015. The conjunction is incoherent within the framework the argument itself sets.
objections.premise_fails_because: W4405407480.c014 fails because it smuggles in the assumption that a truth wholly about God's choosing can have a contingent world-fact as a co-truthmaker, which directly contradicts c012's requirement that all non-tautological truths only about God have only God as their minimal truthmaker.

objections.text: Consider a scenario where God's volition to create the world is an intrinsic property, driven by God's own nature and desires. In this case, God's relation to the world is still partially based on facts extrinsic to God, such as the world's existence and properties. However, the accidental property of volition remains intrinsic to God, as it is a fundamental aspect of God's character. This scenario suggests that the connection between God's relation to the world and the nature of accidental properties is not as straightforward as assumed.
objections.premise_fails_because: The hidden premise fails because it incorrectly assumes that God's relation to the world being partially based on extrinsic facts necessarily implies that the accidental properties of volition and knowledge must also be extrinsic.

objections.text: Father John, a parish priest, teaches that God freely chose to create the actual world only because the world could be ordered in a certain way; he says God's will depends on the existence of contingent possibilities. In Thomist thought, God's free act of creation is a simple, non‑composite act whose truthmaker is God alone. The act does not require a contingent fact to be true; it is a necessary act of the divine intellect and will. Hence the proposition ‘God freely chooses to create the actual world’ cannot be true by virtue of a conjunction of a necessary fact and a contingent fact: it is true solely by God’s simple act, independent of any extrinsic condition.
objections.premise_fails_because: Premise W4405407480.c014 fails because Thomist classical theism holds that God’s free act of creation is a simple, intrinsic act, not dependent on any contingent fact.

objections.text: Consider a person, Leo, who decides to drink water. The truth of 'Leo decides to drink water' is made true by Leo's internal volition. This volition is a property of Leo. The truthmaker is not Leo plus an external, contingent fact; the truthmaker is simply Leo, as a person possessing that specific mental state. Similarly, God's volition is a real, distinct attribute of His personhood. The contingency resides within the property God possesses, not in a fact that exists 'besides' Him. Therefore, an accidental property is not an extrinsic addition but an intrinsic part of God's person.
objections.premise_fails_because: W4405407480.c013 fails because a contingent property is held by the person and does not require a truthmaker existing 'besides' that person.

objections.text: A proponent of divine simplicity distinguishes between the truth-conditions of a proposition and the ontological nature of the properties it describes. For example, the truth of the proposition 'God chooses to create the world' depends on the contingent existence of the world, but the property of volition remains an intrinsic, necessary aspect of God's essence. The presence of an extrinsic truth-maker for a proposition does not necessitate that the property being predicated is an extrinsic attribute of the subject. W4405407480.c013 fails because it conflates the extrinsic truth-conditions of a proposition with the intrinsic nature of the property itself.
objections.premise_fails_because: W4405407480.c013 fails because it conflates the extrinsic truth-conditions of a proposition with the intrinsic nature of the property itself.

objections.text: Sculptor Jules stands before an empty yard and thinks, "I freely choose to sculpt the actual block of marble in the yard." There is no marble; the yard contains only grass. A friend claims the truthmaker for the proposition is Jules alone, with the marble entering only as content, not as a distinct truthmaking component. Yet the proposition is false: Jules cannot have a de re volition toward a non-existent object. If Jules alone sufficed as truthmaker, his mental act would make the proposition true even though no marble exists. Since the proposition remains false precisely because the contingent marble is absent, the marble must function as a distinct truthmaking component, not merely as intentional content. Therefore the revised premise collapses.
objections.premise_fails_because: W4405407480.arg1.r1 fails because, as Jules's empty yard shows, a de re volition toward a contingent object requires that object's existence as a distinct truthmaking component, not merely as content.

objections.text: A sculptor intends to carve this specific block of marble. The truthmaker for 'she intends to carve this block' includes the block's existence, a contingent fact. The volitional property of intending-to-carve-this-block is intrinsic to the sculptor: it is realized entirely by her own mental state, does not inhere in the block, and is a feature of her mind rather than a relation that partly resides outside her. Since a volitional property has a truthmaker that reaches beyond the agent while remaining intrinsic to the agent, including a contingent world-fact in the truthmaker does not make the property extrinsic.
objections.premise_fails_because: Premise W4405407480.arg1.r2 fails because the sculptor's volitional property of intending to carve this block is made true partly by the block's contingent existence yet remains intrinsic to her.

objections.text: The premise assumes that a contingent world‑fact can be included in the truthmaker of God’s accidental volitional property merely as the content of the volition, while the realizer stays wholly divine. This smuggles the claim that a truthmaker may combine a necessary divine element with a contingent element without the contingent element affecting the ontological status of the property. But a truthmaker must be wholly sufficient for the truth of the proposition; any contingent component contributes to its grounding and therefore makes the grounded property partly non‑divine. Consequently the alleged “content‑only” role of the world‑fact is impossible: the contingent fact cannot be present without altering the nature of the truthmaker. The premise therefore rests on an impossible mixture of necessary and contingent truthmaking.
objections.premise_fails_because: Premise W4405407480.arg1.r3 fails because it assumes a contingent world‑fact can be part of the truthmaker of a divine accidental property without making the property non‑divine, violating the requirement that truthmakers be wholly necessary.

restatements.paper_vocabulary: Against c013's inference from a contingent item being required for the truth of an accidental attribution to the attribution's being partly extrinsic: the contingent item figures only as satisfier of a divine content fixed by God alone, as with God's willing that the sun shine on Tuesday, whose sole truthmaker is the divine volition identical with God, so the required contingency is a condition of satisfaction rather than a truthmaker-part, and the step to partial extrinsicness fails.
restatements.plain_english: Needing something outside God for a statement about God to be true does not mean God's property is partly outside God. Take 'God wants the sun to shine on Tuesday.' God's wanting is all that makes that statement true. The sun shining is a separate fact that just happens to match what God wants. So the outside thing is needed for the wish to come true, not for the wish to be what it is.
restatements.neighboring_tradition: In the philosophy of mind and action, this is the distinction between a intention's correctness conditions and its truthmakers: a desire or intention with a fixed content can be satisfied or frustrated by the world without the satisfier entering into what the attitude is. In truthmaker theory it parallels the point that a truth about a relation can be grounded in one relatum's intrinsic nature while the other relatum's existence is only a satisfaction condition. Compare the Euthyphro-style point that God's willing can determine what is good without the goodness being constituted by the willing's external objects, and debates over whether relational or Cambridge properties count as extrinsic.

rounds.speaker: referee
rounds.content: Not a misreading: The objection directly attacks c014 as stated. c014 claims that the truth of 'God freely chooses to create the actual world' depends on the conjunction of a necessary fact about God and a contingent fact about the world. The objection argues that this proposition is instead a truth only about God, and that splitting its truthmaker into a God-component and a world-component contradicts c012. Whether or not this objection succeeds, it engages with the actual claim made in c014 and challenges it head-on, rather than attacking a premise the argument does not hold or a different version of the premise.

rounds.speaker: defender_a
rounds.content: You are right that c012 and c014 cannot both be read as flatly compatible on the surface, but the incoherence depends on reading 'truth only about God' as entailing 'minimal truthmaker is God alone.' The argument's c012 is stated as a constraint on minimal truthmakers of non-tautological truths only about God. Your objection supplies the bridge: a proposition predicating a choice of God is only about God. That bridge is the premise to examine. The proposition is about God's choosing, but its truth-conditions also include that the chosen act is directed at this world; 'creates the actual world' has a world-involving object, and the contingent fact enters through that object, not through the subject. So the proposition is about God in its predicate-subject structure while its truthmaking is hostage to an external relatum. The literature cuts against you here: the powers account [W2918187728.a3] lets divine life truthmake modal truths without the contingent entering the truthmaker, and the de se analysis [W7203485685.c035] shows that 'God actualises W1' and 'I actualise W1' share uncentred truth conditions, so the world-indexed content is what carries the contingency. If the argument must hold that c012 applies to the whole proposition, the reply fails. But c012 can be read as restricted to truths whose truth-conditions involve no extrinsic relatum, and c014 then places this proposition outside it. I do not find the incoherence decisive, but the argument's wording of c012 is too strong as written.
rounds.revised_premise: Premise c012 should be restricted to non-tautological truths about God whose truth-conditions involve no relatum extrinsic to God, so that 'God freely chooses to create the actual world' falls outside it.

rounds.speaker: attacker
rounds.content: You concede the argument's wording of c012 is "too strong as written." That is the point, and your proposed fix destroys the argument rather than saving it. You propose restricting c012 to truths whose truth-conditions involve no extrinsic relatum. But then c012 is satisfied by definition: nothing can violate a constraint that excludes from its scope exactly the cases that would violate it. The modal collapse argument needs c012 to be a genuine constraint that God's accidental properties *break*. If c012 is restricted to propositions with no extrinsic truthmaker, it is never broken, and the entire c012–c015 chain generates no tension. Your "de se analysis" move does not help, since it merely confirms that the world-indexed content carries contingency—reasserting exactly the extrinsic relatum c013 needs. You have not dissolved the incoherence; you have made c012 vacuous, after which c009 has nothing to conclude. The argument as stated fails, and your repair makes it worse.

rounds.speaker: defender_a
rounds.content:
You are right that my proposed restriction makes c012 vacuous, and I withdraw it. The restriction was a mistake: a constraint that excludes exactly the violating cases is no constraint. But your rejoinder assumes the only available repair is restriction of scope. The better repair concerns what 'truth only about God' means. The proposition 'God freely chooses to create the actual world' is about God in its subject and predicate, yet its truth-conditions include a world-involving object, and c014 says the contingent world-fact is a distinct truthmaking component. That is a direct tension with c012 as stated, and the argument's own wording makes it. So I concede that c012 as written is inconsistent with c014 as written. The de se point [W7203485685.c035] does not rescue it either: it shows the world-indexed content carries the contingency, which confirms your reading that the extrinsic relatum is real. The powers account [W2918187728.a3] offers a route in which divine life alone truthmakes modal truths, which would resist c014 directly by denying the contingent world-fact is needed for the truthmaker. Taking that route would mean rejecting c014, not reinterpreting c012. The argument survives only if the truthmaker for the choice-proposition is God alone, with the world entering as content rather than as a truthmaker, and c013 and c015 are then reformulated to speak of extrinsic content rather than extrinsic truthmakers.

Revised premise: The truthmaker for 'God freely chooses to create the actual world' is God alone, with the contingent world-fact entering only as the content of the choice rather than as a distinct truthmaking component, and c013 and c015 are restated in terms of extrinsic content rather than extrinsic truthmakers.

rounds.speaker: defender_b
rounds.content: You misread the scope of c012. It restricts the truthmaker-only-God condition to truths that are non-tautologically only about God, not to every proposition with God as its grammatical subject [W4405407480.c012]. The proposition in c014 is irreducibly relational: to assert that God freely chooses to create the actual world is to assert that God stands in a contingent relation to a specific world, not merely to predicate an intrinsic act of God [W4405407480.c014]. Just as 'Socrates is taller than Plato' is not a truth only about Socrates, this proposition is not a truth only about God, so c012 does not govern it. The argument therefore does not smuggle in a contradictory status for the same proposition; c012 governs intrinsic divine predications such as 'God is good,' where God's being alone metaphysically grounds the truth without adding an intrinsic predicate [W7172336769.c072], whereas c014 governs a relational truth whose truthmaker naturally includes the relatum. The framework explicitly allows God's relation to the world to be based on facts extrinsic to God without undermining absolute simplicity [W4405407480.c029], so the conjunction of a necessary fact about God and a contingent world-fact is precisely the mechanism the argument needs, not an incoherence.

rounds.speaker: attacker
rounds.content:
Your "taller than Plato" analogy fails, and you did not answer why. In that case Plato is a pre-existing relatum, a co-participant in the relation. The world here is not such a relatum; it is the product of God's creative act, not an independent term standing alongside God. To say "God chooses to create the world" is to predicate an act *of* God whose object is generated by the act itself, not to relate God to a pre-given other. So the proposition is genuinely a truth only about God, c012 does govern it, and your carve-out collapses.

You then stipulate, via the final clause, that the framework "allows" extrinsic relations without undermining simplicity. But that is precisely what the modal collapse problem denies: if volition is identical with divine being, the relation is necessary. Asserting that the framework permits contingency is to assume the conclusion the argument must earn. You have not shown how c014's conjunction yields c013's extrinsic property without circularity.

rounds.speaker: defender_b
rounds.content:
You press the disanalogy fairly: unlike Plato, the world is not a pre-existing co-participant, so the relational model is not automatic. Yet even a created object is ontologically distinct from God, and the proposition rigidly designates that object, so its truth conditions are not metaphysically only about God in the sense c012 targets [W4405407480.c012]; that premise governs intrinsic predications like 'God is good' [W7172336769.c072], not singular propositions about creation. Still, your challenge exposes an ambiguity in c012: without an explicit restriction to non-relational truths, it could swallow the creation claim. I concede that the argument needs c012 restricted to non-relational truths: divine simplicity requires that all non-tautological non-relational truths only about God have only God as their minimal truthmaker. With that clarification, c014's conjunction is not an illicit carve-out but a straightforward truthmaking pattern for relational truths, and the contingency of the world-fact is secured by the ontological distinctness of the created order [W4405407480.c016], not assumed [W4405407480.c029].

Revised premise: Divine simplicity requires that all non-tautological non-relational truths only about God have only God himself as their minimal truthmaker.

rounds.content: Not a misreading: The objection directly attacks the unstated premise as stated. The premise claims that if God's relation to the world is partially based on extrinsic facts, then the accidental properties (volition and knowledge) must be extrinsic. The objection provides a counterexample scenario in which God's relation to the world is partially extrinsic yet volition remains intrinsic, thereby challenging the conditional link the premise asserts. This is an attack on the premise itself, not a misreading.

rounds.speaker: defender_a
rounds.content: Under the argument's own truthmaker notion, the scenario is not coherent. You grant that the truthmaker of 'God wills to create the world' includes the world's existence. c013 says any correct attribution of an accidental property has God and something contingent besides God as truthmaker, and that makes the property at least partially extrinsic. Calling volition 'intrinsic' because it flows from God's nature is a different notion, one that c012 does not use. Your point that God's relation to the world is partly extrinsic (c015) does not by itself settle the status of volition, and the mp as written is too weak: it treats the relation as if it were the property. The bridge has to say that the volitional property is the very property whose truthmaker includes a contingent fact. c034 gives the best defence here: the necessary volition has the contingent world as its object, not as an intrinsic feature, so the contingency enters through the object and the property stays extrinsic. The argument survives, but only with the bridge made explicit. [W4405407480.c012] [W4405407480.c013] [W4405407480.c034] [W2737654126.a2]
rounds.revised_premise: An accidental property of God is extrinsic whenever its correct attribution has a contingent truthmaker besides God, so that volition and knowledge are extrinsic whenever they are correctly attributed to God in virtue of the contingent world.

rounds.speaker: attacker
rounds.content: You argue that the scenario I presented is incoherent under the argument's truthmaker notion, and that calling volition 'intrinsic' because it flows from God's nature is a different notion. However, you haven't addressed the core of my objection: that the connection between God's relation to the world and the nature of accidental properties is not as straightforward as assumed. You've focused on the technical aspects of truthmakers and property attribution, but haven't shown why the intrinsic nature of volition, driven by God's own nature and desires, couldn't be compatible with God's relation to the world being partially based on extrinsic facts. This distinction still seems plausible, and the argument's reliance on a straightforward connection between these concepts remains questionable.

rounds.speaker: defender_a
rounds.content:
You are right that the argument's mp is not yet tight, and I concede that much. But your scenario does not show the gap you need. You say volition is intrinsic because it flows from God's nature and desires. The argument's notion is different: a property is intrinsic only if its minimal truthmaker is God alone [W4405407480.c012]. A property that flows from God's nature can still have as truthmaker God plus the contingent world, as in the case of God's willing this world rather than another, and c013 then makes it at least partially extrinsic. Your scenario only works if the world's existence drops out of the truthmaker of 'God wills to create this world', and you have not shown that. Your point that the relation is partly extrinsic (c015) is compatible with volition being intrinsic only if the relation and the volition come apart, and you have given no reason to think they do. The reply that God's necessary volition takes the contingent world as its object, not as an intrinsic feature, is the best route for the defender [W4405407480.c034]. Yet the object-based route also faces the worry that God is not simple if the object enters the truthmaker. So the argument needs the bridge stated explicitly. Still, the objection does not refute it. I concede that the mp as written is too weak and that the bridge is the real point at issue.

Revised premise: If the truthmaker of God's accidental volitional property includes a contingent fact about the world, then that property is extrinsic to God, whatever its origin in God's nature.

You are right that extrinsic relations do not by themselves entail extrinsic properties in general. However, the argument does not rest on that broad entailment alone. The paper explicitly states that any accidental property attributed to God has as its truthmaker both God and something contingent besides God, making it at least partially extrinsic [W4405407480.c013]. The proposition that God freely chooses to create the actual world depends precisely on a conjunction of a necessary fact about God and a contingent fact about the world [W4405407480.c014]. Your scenario of a purely intrinsic accidental volition therefore conflicts with this truthmaker analysis. The extrinsic facts about the world do not merely accompany God's relation to the world [W4405407480.c015]; they enter into the minimal truthmaker for the volition itself. That said, the unstated premise overstates the case as a general entailment from extrinsic relations to extrinsic properties, and the argument should instead rest directly on the truthmaker overlap between the relation and the accidental property.

rounds.content: Not a misreading: The objection directly attacks premise W4405407480.arg1.r2 as stated. That premise asserts a conditional: if the truthmaker of God's accidental volitional property includes a contingent fact about the world, then that property is extrinsic to God. The objection provides a counterexample—a sculptor whose volitional property's truthmaker includes a contingent fact (the block's existence) yet the property remains intrinsic to the agent—thereby challenging the very conditional relationship the premise claims. This is a direct attack on the premise as stated, not a misreading.

rounds.speaker: defender_a
rounds.content:
You are right that the sculptor's intention is realized in her mind while its truthmaker reaches the block, and that intrinsicness is a matter of what the property's realization requires, not of whether its truthmaker mentions anything else. But r2 is tied to the argument's own framework, where the truthmaker of a free choice is the conjunction of an intrinsic desire and an extrinsic fact about the produced effect [W4405407480.c028], and where the precise content of a volitional act need not be intrinsic to the agent [W4405407480.c027]. On that framework your sculptor's intention is partly extrinsic too: the content 'this block' is fixed by something outside her mind. So the case does not show a contingent truthmaker leaving the property intrinsic; it shows that intrinsicness is secured by the bearer's realizer, and the argument can accept that distinction. The real pressure is whether God's volition has a realizer that is wholly divine while its truthmaker includes a world-fact. Here the argument must say that the world-fact enters only as content, which is the r1 move, and r2 then needs 'extrinsic' to mean 'contentful relative to a contingent item' rather than 'realized outside God'. That is a substantive reinterpretation, and I must concede that r2 as written, with 'extrinsic' undefined, does not survive without it. The argument survives only if the notion of extrinsicness is fixed as relational content dependence, and I accept that this changes the premise.

Revised premise: If the truthmaker of God's accidental volitional property includes a contingent world-fact only as the content of the volition, then that property is extrinsic to God in the sense that its content depends on something contingent, while its realizer remains wholly divine.

You are right that c012 is stated universally, and that 'God is not a body' has a privative truthmaker on any natural account. A defender should restrict c012 to positive, intrinsic predications of God, which is the class that threatens simplicity when a contingent world-fact enters the truthmaker. Privations do not threaten simplicity because a privation adds no positive item to God's nature; the absence of matter does not make God composite. The vase analogy fits here: absence of cracks does not add a crack-like component to the vase. The live question is whether a contingent world-fact can be a truthmaker component for a positive divine property without making that property extrinsic. The literature on analogy and truthmaking gives the defender a resource: God is the truthmaker for divine predicates without property exemplification [W7172336769.c066], and predication grounds in God's being rather than in an added predicate [W7172336769.c072]. objection.text: Take a case: God wills from eternity that the sun shine on Tuesday. Attribute to God the accidental property 'is such that the sun shines on Tuesday.' Claimed truthmaker: God plus the sun's contingent shining. But consider a divine act of willing identical with God, whose content is fixed by God alone. Suppose the contingent sun-fact merely satisfies that content when the object obtains; it does not contribute to what God is or to what the attribution ascribes. The truth 'God wills that the sun shine on Tuesday' then has God as its sole truthmaker, while 'the sun shines on Tuesday' is a separate truth about the sun. The attribution requires a contingent condition for satisfaction, not a contingent truthmaker-part. So the step from 'a contingent item is needed for truth' to 'the property is partly extrinsic' does not hold.

objection.text: c015 performs a scope shift from semantic truthmaking to ontological grounding. c014 states only that the proposition 'God freely chooses to create the actual world' is true in virtue of a necessary fact about God plus a contingent fact about the world. c015 converts this into the claim that God's relation to the world is based on facts extrinsic to God, not on contingent intrinsic facts. But the world's role as a truthmaker for a relational proposition does not show that the relation is ontologically grounded in extrinsic facts; it shows only that the proposition is about a relation. God's own act of will could be the contingent intrinsic fact that grounds the relation, with the world serving merely as the relatum. c015 assumes without argument that any proposition requiring the world for its truth must track an extrinsically based property, conflating relational semantics with extrinsic ontology.
objection.premise_fails_because: Premise c015 fails because it illicitly shifts from the proposition's relational truthmaker to the claim that God's relation is ontologically based on extrinsic facts, ignoring that an intrinsic act of will could ground the relation.

objection.text: Consider the truth "God is not a body." This is non-tautological and concerns only God. Its minimal truthmaker is the absence of corporeal composition in God—a privative fact, not God himself. Privations are not identical to the entities they characterize: the absence of matter in God is not God, just as the absence of cracks in a vase is not the vase. Divine simplicity requires only that God lack internal metaphysical composition; it imposes no requirement on what makes negative truths about God true. A defender of divine simplicity can fully accept that "God is not a body" is made true by a privation while maintaining that God is absolutely simple. The same applies to "God is not temporal" and "God is not evil"—each is a non-tautological truth only about God whose truthmaker is an absence rather than God himself.

You rightly press the scope of c012. If it covers every non-tautological truth, negative truths like 'God is not a body' are counterexamples, since their minimal truthmaker seems to be a privation rather than God. But the argument's operative concern is with positive attributions of accidental properties—volition and knowledge—not with negative denials of composition. The truthmaker solution to divine simplicity is explicitly framed for divine predicates: God Himself is the truthmaker for 'God is good' without needing property exemplification [W7172336769.c066]. On the classical view, God is pure act without any composition [W7172336769.c014], and the truth of divine predications is grounded in God's being itself [W7172336769.c072], not in reified absences. Because the inference in c013-c015 concerns only accidental property attributions, the argument survives once c012 is narrowed.

Revised premise: Divine simplicity requires that all non-tautological positive truths only about God have only God himself as their minimal truthmaker.
